missing_primary_keys.caveat: Adding a primary key rebuilds the table: it takes time and free disk space for a new copy of the table, and replicas run the same ALTER after it finishes here, so they lag while they rebuild. ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE makes the server refuse instead of blocking writes when it cannot do it online, for example with a FULLTEXT or SPATIAL index, or when columns must become NOT NULL outside strict SQL mode. Adding an AUTO_INCREMENT column always blocks writes (LOCK=SHARED). The ALTER waits for transactions that use the table, and queries on it queue behind that wait. Try it on a copy or a replica first.

missing_primary_keys.why: InnoDB clusters the rows on a hidden 6-byte row ID (DB_ROW_ID) that queries and tools cannot use. It comes from one counter shared by every table that has no key, and each new ID takes InnoDB's global dictionary mutex, so inserts into all such tables contend for it. Unique keys that cannot stand in: uk_lower ((lower(`s`))): a functional key part. Without a key, a replica applying row-based changes has to search the table to find the changed rows (see Why a primary key matters).

missing_primary_keys.caveat: Adding a primary key rebuilds the table: it takes time and free disk space for a new copy of the table, and replicas run the same ALTER after it finishes here, so they lag while they rebuild. ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE makes the server refuse instead of blocking writes when it cannot do it online, for example with a FULLTEXT or SPATIAL index, or when columns must become NOT NULL outside strict SQL mode. Adding an AUTO_INCREMENT column always blocks writes (LOCK=SHARED). The ALTER waits for transactions that use the table, and queries on it queue behind that wait. Try it on a copy or a replica first.

fixes.label: Declare uk_b as the primary key
fixes.sql: ALTER TABLE `mftab`.`two_uk` ADD PRIMARY KEY (`b`), DROP INDEX `uk_b`, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;

missing_primary_keys.why: InnoDB clusters the rows on uk_b (b), in key order the first unique key on NOT NULL columns, which acts as the primary key. Replicas and tools that need a unique key can use it, but some checks look for a PRIMARY KEY only. Declaring it as the primary key makes that explicit.

notes: Row counts, sizes and free space come from a cache MySQL keeps for up to 1 d 0 h (information_schema_stats_expiry; partitioned tables are never cached), so they can be that old. Fresh numbers (--fresh) reads them from InnoDB now, for myflames' own connection only.

TABLE_ROWS, DATA_LENGTH and INDEX_LENGTH are InnoDB estimates from its table statistics, recalculated in the background after about 10% of the rows change (persistent statistics, the default) or by ANALYZE TABLE. DATA_FREE is read with the other statistics, so it comes from the same cache unless Fresh numbers is on. It counts whole free extents and the unused space at the end of the file (an extent is 1 MiB with 4 to 16 KiB pages, 2 MiB with 32 KiB, 4 MiB with 64 KiB), minus a reserve of 2 extents plus about 1%; free pages in partly used extents and half-empty pages after scattered deletes are not in it, so it understates.
1 table is not InnoDB: listed under missing primary keys when they lack one, never under free space (DATA_FREE means something else for other engines).
Read every schema except mysql, sys, performance_schema and information_schema.

rules.free: watch when free space is at least 10% of the tablespace file and at least 100.0 MiB; problem at 25% and 1.0 GiB
rules.no_usable_key: problem: no PRIMARY KEY and no UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns
rules.not_null_unique: watch: no PRIMARY KEY, but a UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns stands in for it

shared_tablespaces.name: innodb_system
shared_tablespaces.why: Up to 6.0 MiB free in the system tablespace innodb_system, which holds 1 table in scope. DATA_FREE shows that tablespace's free space for each table in it, so it is not per table. Rebuilding a table there frees pages inside the tablespace for reuse; the file does not shrink.

shared_tablespaces.name: mf_gen
shared_tablespaces.why: Up to 7.0 MiB free in the general tablespace mf_gen, which holds 2 tables in scope. DATA_FREE shows that tablespace's free space for each table in it, so it is not per table. Rebuilding a table there frees pages inside the tablespace for reuse; the file does not shrink.

why.text: With row-based replication (the default) each UPDATE or DELETE reaches the replica as the changed rows, and the replica has to find each one. With a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns that is one index lookup per row. Without one, MySQL hashes the rows of each event and looks them up through another index if there is one, or else makes up to one full table scan per event. An event holds about 8 KiB of rows (binlog_row_event_max_size), so a large DELETE means many full scans and the replica falls behind.
why.title: Replicas find each changed row by its key

why.text: InnoDB keeps each table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key, and every secondary index stores the primary key to reach the row. Without a primary key it uses the first unique key on NOT NULL columns (whole columns, not a prefix, a functional part or a virtual generated column). Without one it adds a hidden 6-byte row ID.
why.title: InnoDB stores rows in primary key order

why.text: Queries and tools cannot see or use the hidden row ID to find, page through or deduplicate rows. It comes from one counter shared by every table that has no key, and each new ID takes InnoDB's global dictionary mutex, so inserts into all such tables contend for it.
why.title: The hidden row ID

why.text: Group Replication refuses writes to a table without a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns: the client sees "The table does not comply with the requirements by an external plugin."
why.title: Group Replication needs a primary key

why.text: pt-online-schema-change and gh-ost copy rows in chunks by a primary or unique key; per their documentation they refuse a table without one, so the server's own online ALTER is the only online option left.
why.title: Online schema change tools need a key
